generatedProse.concept-context: Your department confirms the referencing style, and once it is set the task is to apply it to every citation and reference without slips. Subjects in the School of Sport do not all use the same style: sport science often uses an author-date style, while clinical sport therapy may use a numbered one. A marker reads your reference list to judge how widely you have read, and often turns to it first. Where claims rest on evidence, from lab studies to participation data, a full and consistent list shows the scope of your research.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport management students hand in essays, each with a reference list.

Tom has read widely, but his reference list mixes styles. Some entries give the year in brackets and others do not; some article titles are in italics and others in quotation marks; one citation uses a number. The marker cannot tell at a glance how carefully the sources were handled, and the inconsistency undercuts otherwise good research.

Amara has read the same sources and used one style throughout. Every citation matches a full reference, every reference follows the same pattern, and the list is alphabetical. The marker sees the scope of her reading at once, and the consistency reads as care and competence.

Both students did the reading. Only Amara's referencing let the marker see it.
generatedProse.summary: A referencing style is a set of rules for laying out citations and references, and your department will confirm which one your subject uses. What matters most is consistency: one style, applied to every citation and reference. Done well, your reference list shows a marker the scope and care of your research, and earns marks against the criteria. You can now cite, reference and apply a style with purpose across your sport writing.

check.body: In the worked example, why did Amara's reference list work in her favour with the marker?

It placed the references at the start of the essay.
